newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU approves Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger.
newsitem.headline: EU approves Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger.

text.p: The European Commission recommended approval of Boeing Co.'s planned $15 billion acquisition of McDonnell Douglas Corp. Wednesday after the Seattle-based aircraft maker offered last-minute concessions.
"There was a broad agreement (within the Commission). The remedies the Commission was striving for have largely been supplied," EU Competition Commissioner Karel van Miert told a news conference.

The Commission, the European Union's 20-member executive body, said it would send its recommendation -- which averts the danger of a potentially damaging trans-Atlantic trade war -- to antitrust experts from the bloc's 15 countries, who will review it by next week.
In Washington, President Clinton expressed pleasure with the outcome, which he had lobbied for this week.
"I am pleased that Boeing and the EU have resolved their differences. We hope that the EU will give the merger final approval expeditiously," Clinton said in a written statement.
"The Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger will promote consolidation and efficiency in the U.S. defence industry and preserve the jobs of 14,000 workers at Douglas Aircraft Co."
Boeing denied, however, that Clinton or other government officials put any pressure on the company to make concessions.

"We were in contact with the administration on a continuous basis to make sure that they were apprised of where we were but the negotiation was ours," Boeing Chairman Phil Condit told a press conference on Wednesday.
Van Miert said the commission would issue its final decision next week and that he was confident a majority of national experts would back the Commission.

Boeing, already the world's leading aircraft manufacturer, made a last-ditch offer on Tuesday to cancel exclusive supply deals with three U.S. airlines, and refrain from making similiar deals over the next 10 years. That allowed Van Miert to claim victory instead of going ahead with his threat to block the deal and risk a trade battle with Washington.
A Boeing executive, however, said giving up the exclusive aircraft supply deals was the least painful option open to Boeing in securing EU approval for the deal.

Executive Vice President Richard Albrecht said the deals to supply Continental Airlines Inc., Delta Air Lines Inc. and AMR Corp.'s American Airlines with more than 1,200 aircraft over the next 25 years remained largely intact.

"Unless you hear something from them, you should assume that the contracts we have previously negotiated are still, in their essential terms, in effect," Albrecht said. "The only qualifier would be the public undertaking we have made not to enforce our exclusive arrangements."

Boeing had signed deals to supply its planes exclusively to the three carriers for more than 20 years, effectively snuffing out the challenge of its main rival, Europe's Airbus Industrie consortium, in large chunks of the U.S. market.
"It is a key problem. You're closing off an important part of the market," van Miert said. "This was a vital battle in terms of competition policy."
Airbus said it would not not have any response to the decision until it studied the details. But a company spokesman denounced the United States for its stance in the affair.
"Airbus Industrie regrets the arrogant and confrontational attitude of the U.S.A. in these discussions," Alain Dupeich said by telephone from Toulouse, France.
"The unnecessary tension could have been avoided had Boeing proposed true remedies to contentious points raised by the commission at the outset of the talks," Dupiech added.

Boeing also agreed to free up licenses and patents from McDonnell Douglas' military research programmes to rival firms. The commission had argued Boeing could use government funds to subsidise commercial aircraft development.
In another concession, the U.S. aircraft giant undertook not to abuse its dominant market position to influence the important aircraft supplies sector.

Van Miert said he was concerned that the new combined company could persuade suppliers not to cooperate with Airbus, adding that this part of the deal would be monitored closely. Airbus is operated by a consortium of French, British, German and Spanish firms.

German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said he was happy a trade war had been averted but that Boeing would dominate the aerospace industry despite the concessions, making it necessary to restructure Airbus.
"The first step must be a reorganization of Airbus Industrie from a loose consortium to a unified corporation, at best in the form of a public company," he said.
Financial analysts had mixed opinions on whether the Boeing concessions were important or just a bargaining chip.
"The economic effect of these deals will continue even if the (exclusive) terms get dropped from the contracts," said Chris Avery at the Paribas brokerage in London.
In fact, Continental said it did not intend to drop plans to buy aircraft exclusively from Boeing.

The EU executive can reject major mergers if it finds they can harm fair competition in the 15-nation bloc. In the Boeing-McDonnell case, Brussels could have levied heavy fines on the new company if it had gone ahead despite an EU ban. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission approved the merger on July 1.
Boeing stock jumped $3 to $59.19 on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was one of the most active issues.
